beats.caption: A BMS watches and runs a building's mechanical and electrical plant
beats.text: A building management system is the network of sensors, controllers and software that runs chillers, pumps, air handlers and meters. In a data center it is the nervous system for everything that is not IT: the plant that keeps the racks cool and powered.

beats.caption: Thousands of sensors report temperature, flow, pressure and power
beats.text: Every chiller, pump, valve and air handler carries sensors wired to field controllers (DDC panels) over protocols like BACnet and Modbus. A large site has tens of thousands of points, each sampled every few seconds and logged for trends and audits.

beats.caption: Controllers run the control loops; the screen shows one view of the site
beats.text: Field controllers run local loops on their own: hold supply water at a setpoint, stage chillers, vary pump speed. The supervisory layer collects all of it into one plant graphic with trends, schedules and energy reports, often beside the power monitoring and DCIM tools.

beats.caption: When a reading drifts, it raises an alarm and can reset setpoints
beats.text: If chilled-water supply creeps above its band or a pump trips, the BMS alarms, can bring a standby unit online and pushes new setpoints out to the controllers. Good tuning also saves energy: raising water temperatures and trimming fan speeds lowers PUE.

beats.caption: AI sites need more controls, and the same vendors supply them
beats.text: Liquid cooling adds CDUs, more pumps and tighter loops, so control points per MW rise. BMS vendors: Johnson Controls (JCI, Metasys), Schneider Electric (SU.PA, EcoStruxure), Siemens (SIE.DE, Desigo), Honeywell (HON). Software is sticky: once a site is wired to one system it rarely switches.
